review: Fun cyberpunk deckbuilder.  Interesting to see a game like this without rogue-like elements.

Juego de construcción de mazos bastante clásico que recuerda mucho a Magic the Gathering Shandalar.

Hay que tener en cuenta que este juego es anterior a la revolución que supuso Slay the Spire en este género, y por tanto es más un Magic/Hearthstone simplificado (incremento de un punto de energía por turno, máximo de 4 slots para agentes y 3 para poderes).

El sistema de juego, pese a su extremo parecido con MtG, tiene un pequeño toque que lo hace diferente con las habilidades de hackeo.

Al juego le veo dos problemas principales que le hacen perder puntos:

1- La variedad de cartas es reducida (o al menos así me lo parece tras 5 horas de juego). Aunque existen familias de cartas (Corporación, Anarquía, Ley, etc), no existen apenas cartas que aprovechen estos efectos. Tampoco voy a admitir que he tengo la baraja perfecta (ni en broma), pero su calidad parece derivar más del poder de cartas individuales que de sinergias.

Dado que la campaña radica en ir obteniendo nuevas cartas para personalizar nuestro mazo, resulta un poco desperdicio el que realmente no importe mucho la estrategia de construcción del mismo (sí que importa encontrar las cartas buenas).

2- La campaña tiene un salto de dificultad importante en las primeras misiones. No sólo porque la IA sepa lo que hace, sino porque tiene unas cartas muchísimo mejores que las nuestras. Se siente realmente injusto porque no tenemos el acceso a esas cartas hasta mucho más adelante, y puede provocar que nuestros intentos estén condenados al fracaso, dependiendo mucho del RNG.

Tras conseguir alguna carta un poco mejor deja de ser así y las cosas están más igualadas.

En resumen, un intento aceptable de hacer un Magic con campaña single player (y no hay muchos), pero se queda algo corto y podía haber aspirado a más.

It's a neat idea for a deck builder card game with cyberpunk narrative, but the balance is just too awful to enjoy. Short version: going 2nd is a crippling disadvantage, not taking simultaneous damage is a mistake, and getting better cards takes far too long.

Mostly, it's that it has no idea how tempo works, and the reasons other card games do what they do to create a fair experience. Winning the coin flip for 1st turn is a MASSIVE advantage, because you get to place minions first and are always 1 mana/resource point ahead. In a game like Hearthstone, the 2nd place player gets one extra card plus a card that gives 1 mana so they get one turn of being on parity with the 1st player. Despite this, going 2nd in Hearthstone is still a significant disadvantage.

System Crash 2nd player? Gets an extra card and that's it. An already significant disadvantage in other card games turns into a MASSIVE one here. It's to the point where you might as well keep restarting a match until you go 1st, because going 2nd is a waste of time and will result in a loss the large majority of the time.

Compounding that is that attacking minions take no return damage when hitting an enemy minions; they only dish out damage. So going 1st gets yet another advantage of not only being 1 mana ahead all game, but one attack round of free damage as well. This also makes the haste/charge ability (attack the same turn a minion is played) super overpowered since it's a free hit. In Hearthstone, not only does the charging unit still take return damage, but its stats are weaker than a typical non-charge unit of the same cost. System Crash? All the haste/charge minions are the same stats as non-haste units. Nobody balanced this.

Then there's the way targeting works. Instead of any minion being able to target anyone, they are divided into 4 rows and only attack the minion in the same row. What makes this a problem is the VERY widespread "hacking" ability, which automatically fills up your victory points every turn the minion simply exists. Just plunk down your hacking minions across from the lowest damage enemy minions and you're almost untouchable as you rake in free victory points every turn. Try to get around this, and there are still cards that grant the hacking ability to ANY unit. The hacking units also aren't that fragile even if you do hit them.

So just build a good deck on these terms? That's the final nail in the coffin. Getting new cards is GLACIALLY slow. To the point that it feels like this started as a free to play pricing model designed to push you towards spending real money to skip the grind, but at the least minute made it a paid commercial game. Do you want to grind out 40 matches for a single good card? I sure don't. Worse, there are a lot of themed cards that show how rushed and unfinished the game is, because for every themed group that gives bonuses for every matching themed minion, there are only ever 3-5 cards in that group in the ENTIRE game. Trying out any themed deck means doing the above grind 3-5 times. Think that sounds fun? I sure don't.

Finally, while there's no direct proof that the computer cheats, it seems to ALWAYS have good cards to play every turn. Out of the nearly one hundred matches I played, I think the computer had ONE turn where it couldn't play anything. I suspect that its "hand" of cards is a lie, and that it simply has access to its entire deck to play one every turn. It will always have good low cost cards to play in the early turns, and high cost cards to play in later turns. That's not simply good deck construction. Even the best decks will whiff on a draw from time to time. To only whiff ONCE out of 600-700 turns? There's something fishy going on. And it would be one thing if the game got this difficult in the later campaign missions, but it's like this from the THIRD mission. Immediately after the two tutorial missions, you're thrown into the cheating deep end.

I really wanted to like this for the setting and narrative too. But dang it all feels like a cargo cult understanding of card game design.

Decent enough cyberpunk aesthetics and story, but the gameplay is absolutely garbage if you have played more than a couple card games. The most basic possible mechanics, four lanes that autoattack with mana that scales automatically each turn, draw 1 per turn. Pretends to have more going on but the "objective" system is literally just life points but they count up instead of down. I had hopes from the intro, but every mechanical explanation depressed me further. Additionally, for a single player game, the drip of new cards is absolutely pathetic. It takes a couple dozen missions to be able to do anything you might reasonably call "deckbuilding", and meaningful synergies are at least 8-10 HOURS in. 

In the finer points, the hard control cards are also maddening. At the beginning there aren't that many, although the control for support cards is ubiquitous among the opponents, so playing the expensive ones is largely pointless. After you get to the point of ramp cards, hard unit removal, and lots of haste (no summoning sickness) cards showing up, it starts to feel more and more pointless to try and develop a board. The deckbuilding interface is also trash, with no search function for attributes, so building based on the synergies that exist is an absolute chore, and rebuilding your deck for specific enemy challenges is a pain in the ass. I was immediately turned off by the mechanics of this game, but I felt I had to give it a fair shake before leaving a negative review. The lazy card game mechanics just keep coming. Unless it's hiding 12+ hours in, there is nothing of interest you could find in this game that hasn't been done a thousand times in better ones.

Here are several much, much better games you could go play right now:
Faeria
Solforge Fusion
Runescape Chronicles (there's a fan run free version even since it's dead)
Netrunner (physical, still worth it, and if you want the cyberpunk theme, there's none better)

Highly recommended!

For me, this is one of the better CCGs:
- intuitive to pick up, there's quite some variation in cards and effects but nothing crazy (not like some not to be named CCGs that require a 15 page glossary to play)
- the mix between combat damage and "hacking points" is brilliant, it avoids that whoever drops the biggest creatures wins and also forces a certain pace in the rounds
- the layout is clear and works beautifully
- once you get past the initial rounds and have some credits to spend on customizing your deck, it becomes much more interesting and gameplay becomes much more varied; the initial rounds of both campaigns can be tough but a little deck adjustment goes a long way
- everything in the game from the story to the artwork, the cards and their effects all fits perfectly with the cyberpunk theme

RNG does have a significant impact but there's no penalty for losing a battle and the rounds are quite fast, so it's not that big of a deal.
There's the occasional hiccup when the game locks up but for the same reason, this is not a big problem.

I would have loved to have a few more campaigns (still need to try the Underworld DLC) but then again, I'm sure I will play though them several times more, trying different decks and approaches. And the arena mode is ideal if you only have a few minutes to kill.

J'appréhendais beaucoup lors de l'achat de ce jeu, tout d'abord parce qu'il est entièrement en anglais (et que le vocabulaire de hacking et de cyber-infiltration est très spécifique), mais également parce que les "card battler games" ne sont pas tous égaux et captivants.

Et pourtant ce jeu est excellent, je ne le lâche plus depuis quelques jours.

Pour ce qui est de l'anglais, il y aura 2 aspects:
-d'un côté les cartes qui elles seront très simples à comprendre;
-de l'autre côté le jeu en lui même (histoire) qui là demandera un niveau plus exigeant.

Pour ce qui est des matchs, étant un ancien joueur de "Magic the Gathering", qui est un jeu très complexe (attention je ne dis pas "compliqué" mais "complexe", c'est à dire qu'il y aura moult informations à retenir), ici nous sommes dans un jeu bien plus simples à comprendre, mais diablement efficace.

Comme pour bien des jeux de cartes à construire vous aurez des communes (cartes "basic", paquets "bronze"), des unco (cartes "Veteran", paquets "argent"), et enfin des cartes rares (cartes "Elite", paquets or).
Les decks devront avoir une taille minimum de 40 cartes, et pas de limite max. (mais les bons joueurs qui tireront partie des probabilités vous diront tout le temps qu'il faut toujours se rapprocher du cap de cartes, c'est à dire ici de 40 cartes).

Le thème du jeu se situe dans un futur très proche (en réalité une pure dystopie), où des factions séditieuses appelées les "runner" affrontent le nouvel ordre (les "Corps") qu'ils rejettent, ils proposent ainsi leurs services auprès du plus offrant pour les voler (hacking); le jeu étant empreint de culture japonaise, on y retrouvera donc une faction de Yakuza en plus des runners, mais également des anarchistes, des criminels (non Yakuzas), des robots (les "Mechs") ou encore les fameux "Corps" et ceux travaillant pour la loi ("Law agents").

Le jeu ressemble beaucoup à "Magic" (sans l'heroic fantasy) en plus simple, vous aurez les agents qui ont des caractéristiques basiques comme l'attaque (représentée par une balle de revolver), la défense (qui enlève de l'attaque), le coût de la carte en crédit (on gagne 1 cr. par tour, max. 10), 3 places sur le côté de chaque agent pour des boosts et 3 autres pour des contraintes. En bas du board vous aurez 3 places pour y placer des cartes "support" qui dureront un certain nombre de tours et ou aideront vos forces ou bien gêneront l'ennemi, puis à cela rajoutez des cartes à effet immédiat qui partent ensuite dans la défausse (events).

Votre main ne pourra avoir plus de 10 cartes (après on défausse) et on pioche 1 carte par tour.
Enfin pour ce qui est de la construction de deck, ce sera 4 exemplaires max. de la même carte sauf certaines qui sont illimitées (il y en a peu).
Vous pourrez construire et acheter vos cartes au "Black Market", de plus vous en gagnerez à la fin de chaque mission, en plus des crédits.
Une cartes basique coûte 1000 cr et se vend 100 cr, ce sera 2500/500 cr pour une veteran et 10000/2500 pour une elite.

Dans un match vous aurez 4 places pour placer vos agents, idem pour l'ennemi.
Le but est d'atteindre une somme en OP (Operation Points) que vous piratez à l'ennemi, et empêcher que l'ennemi atteigne votre somme max. qui est de 50 OP la plupart du temps.
Pour cela vous devrez donc bloquer ses agents, mais également vous débarrasser de ses cartes supports qui pourront également vous ponctionner.
Si un agent n'est pas bloqué, son attaque passe et il commence à amasser, une fois 50 OP atteint vous perdez.

Le jeu est donc simple mais très prenant, de plus son univers est mâture et sombre.
Un très bon jeu que je recommande vraiment, n'hésitez pas si vous aimez la stratégie et le genre.

Fun card game with a good amount of different mechanics to allow you to make a couple decks. Energy system similar to Hearthstone ( where you start with one and get one more each turn up to 10 ) but to win instead of lowering the opponent HP, you get points by direct damage or can use hacking cards or units and win defensively.

Early on the AI is pretty easy but at some point in the campaign they start having very strong specialised decks so you need to build one to counter their specific strategy or try again and again until you get a lucky game. The AI and the player have the same cards available so it is usually fair but the main module at one point will have special fights with different bonuses.

The Cyberpunk universe is nice, quite a good amount of story to read between the battles and there is the arena if you want to play cards without interruption and win a couple more cards. The UI is a bit simple but it works for what it is.

There seems to be a recurring bug that sometimes all your cards lights up even without the energy but you can't play any and the only option is to forfeit or skip your turn until you lose. It's not that much of a problem since losing a fight has no penalty, you simply start again but it happened about 10 times in the 35 hours I played so it can get a bit infuriating.

I'll start by noting that I've played WAY more than 7 hours of this game. I've played with Steam offline quite a bit is all. There isn't much to say at this point that other reviewers haven't, so I'll keep this short. This is a solid deck-building solo experience in a cyberpunk setting. I thoroughly enjoyed the selection of cards and the freedom to build a number of decks with a number of different effects, as well as the story for the 3 campaigns. One complaint that I do have is a somewhat grindy component (mentioned in other reviews) where you must play in an arena to make money on occasion. It has 3 difficulties, and you have to win 10 matches in the previous difficulty to get to the next. I'd say half that number and it'd be perfect. System Crash is a single-player deckbuilder set in a cyberpunk-style universe.  Battles unfold as a number of 1-vs-1 card-based duels over the course of the campaign.  The campaign follows a comfortably generic story about hackers and back-alley doctors and shady corporations.  There's a very home-brew feel to the game in general, like it was cobbled together out of assets that were sitting around on a shelf in a garage somewhere.

Despite this, the card-battle system at the heart of System Crash is fantastic.  It is extremely easy to pick up, but is highly addictive.  

In battle, each player starts with five cards, and draws one card each turn.  Cards are played onto a battlefield at a cost of AP; the better the card, the more it costs to use.  You have 1 AP on the first turn, 3 AP on the third turn, 9 AP on the 9th turn, and so on; the longer the battle lasts, the more stuff you can do and the more interesting it becomes.

In each battle, the object is to be the first to earn a set amount of points.  Points are generally earned by attacking your opponent, but there is also an extremely powerful deck type called "hacking" which focuses on turtling and winning through the passive generation of points instead of attacking.

Battles generally revolve around pitting your "agent" cards, with attack, armor, and life stats against the enemy's (many have special effects and abilities as well).  To support your agents, you also have cards that can buff or debuff the agents on the field, cards that provide temporary bonuses for your whole army, and single-use cards with a specific instant effect.  There is a huge variety of cards in the game, offering a wide variety of viable builds.

Some of the specialty deck types are extremely fun to play with.  There's the aforementioned hacking, there's a criminal build which offers unstoppable stacking bonuses for each criminal you are able to get into play; there's a runner build which focuses on overwhelming the enemy with many low-cost cards, there's a mech build which takes a while to get off the ground but can end up doing dozens of damage per turn.

You have very limited card types to start, and can unlock more by playing.  New cards come as random drops; once you find one card of any type, you can always buy more in the shop, but they are expensive.  You may end up grinding a bit if there is something specific you want.

[h1] [b]What is this game about?[/b] [/h1] 

A single player card game set in a cyberpunk universe where your main character acts as a runner caught up in, unsurprisingly, a corporate scheme. It hosts a fair number of cards which can build up to several notable type of decks. However, apart from some novel ideas, the card play is not amazing in any way and much of possible decks will be familiar to any card game fan. Still, it's a game that is fun to play for a while, boasting a decent story, even if takes too long to finish and the price is a bit too high for what it is.

[h1][b]The positive[/b] [/h1] 
+ Awesome music. It's that good that it deserves to be mentioned as the first point. 

+ The goal is to reach a certain score first. I liked this small change as it feels fresh compared to "take down your opponent to 0 HP" and it opens up a few more mechanics.

+ The story was enjoyable. The writing was very good, and the storytelling feels fluent, despite the main plotline being more or less a standard one.

+ Great tutorial. A lot of good games ruin a good first impression due to a bad introduction to the main mechanics. This one, though, does it very well and something I wished more designers would take time to do properly. 

+ Cool artwork. Some amazing art in the game done by various artists, with in game attributions.

[h1][b]The neutral[/b][/h1] 
* The deckbuilding and card play is mediocre. While the cards fit the cyberpunk theme well, the decks and card combos feel all too familiar (rush, stall, board control etc)

* All cards are purchasable by ingame currency. You can acquire any card from the market. This can be a positive or a negative depending on the player. Personally, I would've slightly more preferred to naturally build up my deck from card drops, but with all cards being accessible at least you get to try most, if not all, decks the game has to offer before finishing it.

* Disparity between theme and cards played by the enemy. You will see some Security enemies play a rush deck (anarchist cards) or you can use Yakuza minions against Yakuza. Of course this is all abstraction and game mechanics, but it does break immersion a bit.

[h1][b]The negative[/b] [/h1] 
- Overstays its welcome. My biggest negative is that the game dragged on way past the point I felt I have seen all that it had to offer. Yet you were continuously thrown into fight against familiar enemies after you consistently won against them many times before.

- Draw seems too powerful. You only draw one card per turn, so the later rounds of the fight seem to heavily favor the opponent who has more card draw in the deck as paying the cost of cards is no longer a problem. I have won plenty of fights just because the opponent had only one card to play per turn. 

[h1][b]Conclusion:[/b] [/h1] 
A robust but mediocre deckbuilder with good writing that would be a great pass time if it didn't take too long to finish. Still for those hungry for card games, it's a decent choice, especially if caught on sale.

It's not a bad game, but as I've mentioned, it doesn't stand out. If you particularly like the theming or if the game's on a good sale, it can be worth checking out. However, I don't think that's enough for me to recommend it in general.

[i]System Crash[/i] is a cyberpunk-themed card game with simple, but satisfying gameplay mechanics. The game offers an atmospheric cyberpunk setting with great writing, gorgeous art, and a soundtrack that sets the mood perfectly. The UI is probably the weakest aspect of the game with a lack of widescreen support and little to no feedback as to what card is selected, which caused me to play the wrong card by mistake on numerous occasions. Gameplay can also be a victim of RNG at times and some matches require a few retries because of this. I also loved to see a local multiplayer option at least as the game can be immensely fun when played with others, but sadly no form of multiplayer is available. In the end, [i]System Crash[/i] may not be the deepest of collectible card games, but offers a well written cyberpunk story coupled with beautiful artwork, and can keep you entertained for quite some time. I can wholeheartedly recommend the game.

* Damage is permanent and is cumulative from turn to turn. Armor can reduce damage.
* Permanent "enchantments" have a limited duration.
* The pool of money to purchase units increase by 1 each turn. Giving you more powerful units on later turns.
* Victory points are mainly awarded by not being blocked by an opponent in a column, or by having hackers in your team that will harvest Victory points. So you have 2 path to victory here.
* You can acquire cards by winning battle. Once you acquire a card, you can spend credits to buy additional copies. The rarer the card, the more expansive the card.

In general, the game is good for an indie game. The enemy deck can be challenging, there is various path to victory, and you will design different deck for various situations. There has seem to be a lot of effort put into the story, but personnaly, I don't really care about it. It's just text, and your answers don't impact the game, so you can just skip it. 

Else my personal issues I have with the design of this game:

* Card drawing: Like in Magic the gathering, if you draw 1 card per turn, and play more than 1 card per turn, after X turn, you have an empty hand, and end up waiting for the card that makes you win, or lose the game. Now there are a lot of cards that allows you to patch this design issue by making you draw more cards. Make sure those cards are there. You can also take advantage of this against the AI, the the AI deck that does not have any card drawing cards, will end up with an empty hand giving you a chance to take over. A quick fix would have been to draw 2 cards per turn. Or spend a credit to draw a 2nd card. There are various solutions.

* The second issue is the equipments. Character can have equipment cards that will boost their stats. Unfortunately, compared to events and support cards, you need to have a unit in play to attach an equipment card. Without units in play, your equip is useless. Second, many units does not survive more than 2-3 turn, so you will in average benefit from those abilities once or twice per card. Personally, I would have used the Magic the gathering equip system. Where you pay to put it in play, and you pay to attach it to a character. But when the character dies, the equipment remains available to be used again. There are alternatives, like returning equip to hands, having an armory where you can pool equip, etc.

Even with those issues, the game is very much playable.

System Crash is a strategic story-rich cyberpunk card game both developed and published by Rogue Moon Studios. Set in the not too distant future this is a story of intrigue, corporate espionage and cyberwarfare. Being a runner is a good, if not dangerous, career choice but after a mission in Berlin goes horribly bad you spend the next couple of months forcibly globetrotting while on the run from Corporate assassins intent on killing you. Eventually evading the pursuers you finally end up back in the "Sprawl", a.k.a. San Angeles, down on your luck and looking to make some much needed credits. But a runner without a console can't get any credits so after forging a deal with a local loan shark and finally getting your hands on some black market cyberware you hastily start down your road to redemption. A road that will take you through the darkest most dangerous places in both cyberspace and the real world...JACK IN!!!

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

Other than "Shadowhand" and of course "Gwent", I've not had much luck at finding a really good card game that I actually enjoyed playing...until now that is. System Crash is just so much FUN! It's one of those casual games that you can pick up intending to play a hand or two for only a couple of minutes and before you know it an hour or more has quickly gone by. Also, I'm not that bright and I can tell you with ease that I've had a hard time following the tutorials in most of the card games that I previously tried. It's just really hard to truly enjoy a game if you can't get the basics down. However with this title the tutorial was intuitive and after only a couple of battles I was able to grasp the fundamentals of gameplay with ease. 

I'm a big fan of "Puzzle Quest" which is the absolute best match-3 title available. For anyone who is familiar with or has played "Puzzle Quest" I would best describe System Crash as being very similar to it but instead of fantasy and match-3 it's cyberpunk and card battles. Also, the card battling in this title has a very engrossing story wrapped around it but the basic gameplay consists of you getting into combat against various enemies which could include people, mechs or computer systems that need to be hacked in order to accomplish your many objectives. Victory is achieved if you can use the cards in your cyberdeck to defeat your opponents deck so strategy and tactics are vital. The cards themselves are basically characters both human and mech armed with ballistic weapons of varying degrees of lethality. Some have more firepower and health than others. Many cards even have special abilities as well as buffs that can increase the effectiveness of your other cards in play such as increased firepower or additional armor among other attributes. 

During each round you and your opponent are both granted a total number of points that you can use on your turn in battle. All the cards in your hand cost a certain amount of points to play depending on what type of card that it is so you must strategically decide which cards to place and when to place them if you want to come out of the battle victorious. This battle of tactics and strategic matching of wits is the absolute best part of this glorious game. Also, besides the addictive card battle gameplay I would say that the cards themselves are one of the stars of this excellent title. Depending on your particular style of play you can customize your decks using the various types of characters from the game such as the "Runners", the "Anarchists", "Corporate", the "Yakuza" and "MetroSec" a.k.a. the law as well as all the other different program cards, tactical cards, weapon/armor cards and many others. 

The cards have a hierarchy from the Basic or lower level cards to the Veterans which are mid level all the way up to the Elites which are the most powerful, expensive and hardest to acquire cards in the game. Speaking of which, you can get more cards by either buying them on the Black Market with credits that you earn over the course of the narrative or winning them as you defeat various opponents and achieve objectives in the game. The way that you stack your cyberdeck is completely up to your preference and skills. You may also need to specifically tailor a deck with certain cards in order to defeat a particularly difficult opponent as I had to do a couple of times. When it comes down to the overall gameplay I guess the phrase "Easy to learn hard to master" definitely applies to this title.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

This game is simply gorgeous! It has all the visual presentation that you would expect of a cyberpunk title...a dark dystopian future, a huge megalopolis teaming with neon lights, flickering Japanese signage, those awesome flying cars and cool looking but highly dubious characters lurking everywhere. The campaign's story is told through various cutscenes of characters meeting face to face in a variety of locations throughout the city and also in text messages while in cyberspace. Along the way you'll get into intense gun battles in back alleyways with the Yakuza, get hassled by the "man" and just find yourself in all manner of unique predicaments over the course of the terrific narrative. 

The illustrations for both the various locales of the city and the portrait artwork of the many characters in the game are stunningly beautiful while also sticking heavily to the aformentioned cyberpunk theme of the game which is lots of cool haircuts, awesome outfits and augmentations. The U.I. interface for the card battles is highly stylized, expertly laid out and intuitive. All the information that you need is readily visible and you can tab over any card on the battlefield at any time to see it's statistics and what it does which is quite helpful. Overall, I would say that this titles visual presentation is of the highest quality and you can see that the developers put a lot of hard work and effort into this game.

[h1]SOUND[/h1]

The aural presentation in this title is top notch with crisp high fidelity sound effects for the card battles as well as the user interface. Also, the musical score is bursting with cyberpunk inspired tracks that fit the bleak tone of the game perfectly whether you're battling some ruthless mercenaries intent on putting you in a grave or just having chit-chat with a fellow runner in a dark alley as the rain plummets down around you. Overall I'd have to say that the sound quality in this title does a fantastic job of immersing you in the world of cyberpunk. 
 
[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

I'll say the same thing about this game that I did when I came across "Puzzle Quest"...this is indeed one of those "hidden gem" titles that I'm so fond of discovering on Steam. It's always great to acquire a game in your library that will consistently keep you entertained for long periods of time and not just some title that you play once for a few weeks never to pick up again. Aside from the addictive card combat, I also really enjoyed the narrative portion of this game. It takes you on a grand adventure through the city full of intrigue, fascinating characters, gun battles and even adds some much needed comic relief as the nature of the story is often very serious most of the time. 

Replayability is very high because of the dynamic combat and different decks that you can build. D.L.C. comes in the form of the "Deluxe Edition Content" which adds the wonderful soundtrack and high-resolution wallpapers alongside "Underworld" that includes a new campaign. I managed to complete my first playthrough with D.L.C. in just over 49 hours. On the technical side, I experienced a glitch a few times during card battle where the game became unresponsive but this was easily solved with a restart...nothing game breaking. In summary, the cyberpunk themed narrative and fantastic card combat made for a truly thrilling gaming experience so System Crash is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to cyberpunk, card game, strategy and story-rich gamers everywhere!
